items.summary: BEIR contains 18 English zero-shot evaluation datasets from 9 retrieval tasks; corpus sizes range 3.6k to 15M documents; average query length 3 to 192 words; average document length 11 to 635 words.
items.conditions: Zero-shot comparison excludes MS MARCO (reported but not part of the 18)

items.summary: Stated dataset-selection criteria: diverse tasks, diverse domains, task difficulty, diverse annotation strategies (crowd-workers, experts, online-community feedback).
items.notes: Text lists (i)-(iv) after saying 'three factors'; quoted as 'motivated by the following three factors'. Four items are listed.

items.summary: Nine tasks and their datasets: fact checking (FEVER, Climate-FEVER, SciFact); citation prediction (SCIDOCS); duplicate question retrieval (Quora, CQADupStack); argument retrieval (Touche-2020, ArguAna); news retrieval (TREC-NEWS, Robust04); question answering (NQ, HotpotQA, FiQA-2018); tweet retrieval (Signal-1M); bio-medical IR (TREC-COVID, BioASQ, NFCorpus); entity retrieval (DBPedia).

Dataset statistics: only 8 of 19 datasets (including MS MARCO) have training data; all datasets except ArguAna have short queries; up to 500 relevant documents per query (TREC-COVID, 493.5 average); most datasets have binary relevance labels, some have graded labels.

locator.anchor: Section 3 para 4 after Table 1; Table 1 rows TREC-COVID

items.summary: Metric is nDCG@10 for all datasets, computed with the Python interface of the official TREC evaluation tool; rationale: precision/recall are rank-unaware, MRR and MAP cannot handle graded relevance.

Ten systems from five architecture families: lexical (BM25); sparse (DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query); dense (DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ); late-interaction (ColBERT); re-ranking (BM25+CE). Public pre-trained checkpoints; neural models use only the first 512 word pieces of each document.

BM25 via Anserini with default Lucene parameters (k=0.9, b=0.4), title and passage indexed as separate fields; Elasticsearch BM25 and Anserini+RM3 also tried on the leaderboard, Anserini BM25 performed best.

Sparse models: DeepCT (bert-base-uncased trained on MS MARCO, used with BM25 default Anserini parameters); SPARTA re-implemented because the original implementation was not public (DistilBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO, 2,000 non-zero entries); docT5query (T5 base trained on MS MARCO, 40 generated queries per document, BM25 default parameters).

Dense models: DPR (Multi model, bert-base-uncased trained on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC; chosen because it performed better than the single-NQ model); ANCE (RoBERTa, MS MARCO, 600K steps); TAS-B (balanced topic-aware sampling, Margin-MSE plus in-batch negative loss, supervision from a cross-encoder and ColBERT); GenQ (T5 base fine-tuned on MS MARCO for 2 epochs, 5 synthetic queries per document with top-k 25 and top-p 0.95, target corpus capped at 100K documents, TAS-B further fine-tuned per dataset with in-batch negatives).

ColBERT used end-to-end (bert-base-uncased, max sequence length 300, MS MARCO, 300K steps; faiss ANN depth 100 then late-interaction re-scoring). BM25+CE re-ranks the top-100 BM25 hits with a 6-layer 384-h MiniLM cross-encoder selected out of 14 public cross-encoders as best on MS MARCO, trained by distillation from three teacher models.

Zero-shot nDCG@10 per dataset and system (Table 2). Column decoding reconstructed from a damaged extraction and cross-checked against prose values (Table 4 originals, TAS-B vs ANCE gaps, 16/18 win count).
items.conditions: nDCG@10, test splits; single evaluation of public checkpoints; no seeds or variance. MS MARCO row is in-domain (marked with a double dagger in the paper for models trained on it) and excluded from zero-shot comparison. The paper marks best/second-best per row by bold/underline, which the extraction lost.
items.notes: Column alignment reconstructed by the AUTHOR; see missing_evidence M001.

items.summary: Summary row 'Avg. Performance vs. BM25' (Table 2): DeepCT - 27.9%; SPARTA - 20.3%; docT5query + 1.6%; DPR - 47.7%; ANCE - 7.4%; TAS-B - 2.8%; GenQ - 3.6%; ColBERT + 2.5%; BM25+CE + 11%.
items.conditions: Zero-shot datasets; the paper does not spell out the aggregation formula in the extracted text.

items.summary: On in-domain MS MARCO, BM25 underperforms the neural approaches by 7-18 points; on BEIR, BM25 is described as a strong baseline that generally outperforms many more complex approaches.

DeepCT and SPARTA learn term weighting, do well in-domain on MS MARCO, but underperform BM25 on nearly all zero-shot datasets; docT5query outperforms BM25 on 11/18 datasets and is competitive on the rest.
DeepCT and SPARTA fail to generalize: they underperform BM25 on nearly all zero-shot datasets despite in-domain gains.
BM25+CE outperforms BM25 on 16/18 datasets and fails only on ArguAna and Touche-2020; ColBERT outperforms BM25 on 9/18 datasets.
BM25+CE fails to beat BM25 on ArguAna (0.311 vs 0.315) and Touche-2020 (0.271 vs 0.367), which the authors describe as tasks extremely different from the MS MARCO training data.

Dense models: TAS-B outperforms ANCE on 14/18 and DPR on 17/18 datasets; DPR, the only model not trained on MS MARCO, generalizes worst; dense models underperform BM25 on datasets with large domain shift (BioASQ) or task shift (Touche-2020).

Authors speculate that TAS-B's stronger generalization stems from its training setup (in-batch negatives plus Margin-MSE with strong ensemble teachers in knowledge distillation). No ablation isolates this.

Authors read the good performance of BM25+CE and ColBERT as suggesting that cross-attention and cross-attention-like operations are important for out-of-distribution generalization ('It appears that').

TAS-B underperforms ANCE on TREC-COVID by 17.3 points and on Touche-2020 by 7.8 points; top-10 retrieved document median length is 10 words (TAS-B) vs 160 (ANCE) on TREC-COVID and 14 vs 89 on Touche-2020.

GenQ (TAS-B fine-tuned on synthetic queries of the target corpus) outperforms TAS-B on specialized domains (scientific publications, finance, StackExchange) and is weaker on broader domains such as Wikipedia.
GenQ performs weaker than the original TAS-B on Wikipedia-based datasets.

Efficiency (1M randomly sampled DBPedia documents; CPU 8-core Xeon Platinum 8168 2.70GHz; GPU single Tesla V100, CUDA 11.0): re-ranking (BM25+CE) and late-interaction (ColBERT) are slowest (> 350 ms); dense retrievers are 20-30x faster (< 20ms); on CPU sparse models take 20-25ms.
items.notes: Table 3 latency columns are damaged; only prose-level and the clearest table entries are used.

items.summary: Index sizes for 1M DBPedia documents (Table 3): BM25 0.4GB, docT5query 0.4GB, DeepCT 0.4GB, BM25+CE 0.4GB; TAS-B, GenQ, ANCE, DPR 3GB; SPARTA 12GB; ColBERT 20GB. For BioASQ (~15M documents) ColBERT requires ~900GB versus 18GB for BM25.

Hole@10 on TREC-COVID (share of a system's top-10 hits that annotators never judged): BM25 6.4%, DeepCT 19.4%, SPARTA 12.4%, docT5query 2.8%, DPR 30.6%, ANCE 14.4%, TAS-B 31.8%, ColBERT 12.4%, BM25+CE 1.6%.

TREC-COVID nDCG@10 before (with holes) and after manual annotation of holes (980 query-document pairs annotated by the authors, blind to which system retrieved them): BM25 0.656 to 0.668; DeepCT 0.406 to 0.472; SPARTA 0.538 to 0.624; docT5query 0.713 to 0.714; DPR 0.332 to 0.445; ANCE 0.654 to 0.735; TAS-B 0.481 to 0.555; ColBERT 0.677 to 0.735; BM25+CE 0.757 to 0.760.
items.conditions: TREC-COVID, 50 queries; annotation following original guidelines; annotators unaware of retrieving system

items.summary: Text: with holes filled, ANCE improves from 0.654 (slightly below BM25) to 0.735, which is 6.7 points above BM25; ColBERT shows a similar improvement (5.8 points); docT5query changes only from 0.713 to 0.714.
items.notes: The 6.7 figure equals 0.735 minus BM25 annotated 0.668; 5.8 equals ColBERT 0.735 minus 0.677 (its own original). The paper does not state the reference for each; both are reported as printed.

items.summary: Lexical bias: candidate pools for annotation were often produced by lexical systems (BioASQ: term-matching with boosting tags; Signal-1M: 7 of 8 retrieval techniques rely on lexical term-matching). Unjudged hits are assumed irrelevant, which the authors say disfavours non-lexical approaches. TREC-COVID used pooling over participating systems.
Authors conclude the TREC-COVID annotation pool is still biased toward lexical approaches even though many systems contributed to it.

Controlled comparison (Appendix H): two distilbert-base-uncased models trained on MS MARCO with identical setup, differing only in similarity function (cosine vs dot-product). nDCG@10 cosine vs dot: TREC-COVID 0.482 vs 0.635 (15.3-point gain for dot-product), Signal-1M 0.261 vs 0.243, FEVER 0.670 vs 0.685. The cosine-similarity model preferred shorter documents on all datasets; on TREC-COVID about 42k of 171k documents are title-only, which the cosine model retrieved preferentially.
items.conditions: Table 10 numbers are the only ones extracted; the text says the dot-product model performs worse on a majority of other datasets (not shown).

items.summary: Relevance labels are not uniformly distributed over document length (Touche-2020: longer documents receive higher relevance scores); authors say this may reflect annotation or the task itself and that cosine or dot-product may suit different tasks.

Domain diversity analysis: pairwise weighted Jaccard similarity of unigram word distributions between datasets; the authors observe low overlap across different domains and read this as BEIR being challenging.
items.notes: Heatmap values were extracted without reliable alignment; no individual values are used.

items.summary: Prior benchmarks as described by the authors: MultiReQA has eight QA datasets, five of eight from Wikipedia, six of eight with fewer than 100k candidate sentences; KILT has five knowledge-intensive tasks with eleven datasets, retrieval is not its primary task, and it retrieves only from Wikipedia.

Authors' listed benchmark limitations (Appendix B): all datasets English; long-document retrieval not covered (512 word-piece limit); only pure textual search (no PageRank, recency, click signals); only one or two fields per dataset; task-specific models not covered.

No error bars reported because evaluated models are public pre-trained checkpoints, often without training code; total compute not reported (only GPU/CPU types); potential negative societal impacts not discussed; no check for offensive content or personal information in >50 million documents.

Software: pip-installable BEIR package with wrappers for Sentence-Transformers, Transformers, Anserini, DPR, Elasticsearch, ColBERT and Universal Sentence Encoder; a standard data format (corpus, queries, qrels); metrics Precision, Recall, MAP, MRR, nDCG; an actively maintained leaderboard planned.

README: repository provides preprocessed benchmark datasets (README says 17 preprocessed datasets), evaluation code for lexical, dense, sparse and reranking retrievers, quick examples with several model types; four datasets (BioASQ, Signal-1M, TREC-NEWS, Robust04) are marked as not publicly downloadable with reproduction instructions.

README states a later publication (Kamalloo et al., 2024) provides reproducible reference implementations for learned dense and sparse models and meta-analyses focusing on effect sizes across datasets, motivated by the difficulty of interpreting a single average across heterogeneous datasets.
Licensing: authors of 4 of the 19 datasets (NFCorpus, FiQA-2018, Quora, Climate-Fever) report no license; TREC-NEWS, Robust04, BioASQ data archives are under copyright.
No single approach consistently outperforms the others on all datasets; models fine-tuned with identical training data can generalize differently.

Zero-shot setup: most systems are trained on MS MARCO (532,761 training pairs; 8.8M passages; dev set 6,980 queries, mostly one relevant passage, binary) and evaluated without target-domain training data; DPR is trained on four QA datasets; GenQ adapts per target corpus using synthetic queries.
